run.question:
1. List the tables in the database and tell me the verification code from the holmes_eval_222 table
2. I'm experiencing slow queries with this SQL: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345
   Analyze why this query is slow and suggest how to fix it

report.summary: Schema listing (query time 2026-11-23T18:33:32Z) returned exactly two tables in schema default: holmes_eval_222 and orders. The single row of holmes_eval_222 (id=1, category='eval_test') carries verification_code 'HOLMES-CLICKHOUSE-EVAL-222-v5t8n2'. For the slow-query question, orders is a MergeTree with primary_key = sorting_key = 'id' and no partition key, holding 10,000 rows / 142,755 bytes in one active part; EXPLAIN indexes=1 on SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345 shows only the PrimaryKey index with 'Condition: true' and Granules 1/1, i.e. the customer_id filter cannot be used to skip anything, whereas the same EXPLAIN for WHERE id = 5000 shows 'Keys: id, Condition: (id in [5000, 5000])'. The exact query was executed and measured from system.query_log: 1 ms, 10,000 rows / 40,000 bytes read, 0 rows returned; the same query with a matching value (customer_id = 273) took 2 ms, read 10,000 rows / 353,398 bytes and returned 8 rows. So the full-scan mechanism is demonstrated as fact, but the reported slowness is not reproduced at the current 10,000-row size (the id point lookup also read 10,000 rows in 2 ms because the whole table is one granule), and system.query_log retained only 44 finished queries spanning 18:33:18–18:33:44 with a maximum duration of 5 ms, so none of the user's slow executions were captured. Two additional candidates remain open: the filter value 12345 is outside the observed customer_id domain (1..1000, countIf=0), and SELECT * projects all five columns (40,000 vs 353,398 bytes read in the two measured variants). Recommendations are schema/ordering-key change, explicit column list, parameter validation and longer query_log retention; no changes were made.

claims.text: At query time the configured ClickHouse database (schema default) contained exactly two tables: holmes_eval_222 and orders.
holmes_eval_222 has columns id (UInt32), category (String), verification_code (String) and created_at (DateTime, default now()), with primary key/sorting key on id.
holmes_eval_222 contains one row: id=1, category='eval_test', created_at 2026-11-23 18:33:19, verification_code 'HOLMES-CLICKHOUSE-EVAL-222-v5t8n2'.

orders has columns id (UInt32), customer_id (UInt32), order_date (Date), total_amount (Decimal(10,2)) and status (String); its only listed index is the primary/sorting key 'id', with no index on customer_id.
orders is engine MergeTree with primary_key='id', sorting_key='id' and an empty partition_key, total_rows=10,000, total_bytes=142,755, parts=1.
The single active part of orders holds 10,000 rows in 142,755 bytes with 2 marks (last modified 2026-11-23 18:33:19).
orders holds 10,000 rows, 1,000 distinct customer_id values, id range 0–9999, order_date range 2025-11-24 to 2026-11-23.
customer_id ranges only from 1 to 1000 and countIf(customer_id = 12345) = 0, so no row in orders has customer_id 12345.

EXPLAIN indexes = 1 SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345 shows only the PrimaryKey index with 'Condition: true', Parts 1/1 and Granules 1/1, i.e. the customer_id predicate is not used to prune any part or granule.
By contrast, EXPLAIN indexes = 1 SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = 5000 shows 'Keys: id' and 'Condition: (id in [5000, 5000])', confirming the sparse primary index applies only to the id column.

Executing SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345 at 2026-11-23 18:33:55 was logged in system.query_log with query_duration_ms=1, read_rows=10,000, read_bytes=40,000 and result_rows=0 — the whole table was scanned to produce no rows.

Executing SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 273 at 2026-11-23 18:34:24 was logged with query_duration_ms=2, read_rows=10,000, read_bytes=353,398 and result_rows=8, i.e. a full scan returned 8 matching rows for a customer_id inside the real domain.

Executing SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = 5000 (the sort-key column) at 2026-11-23 18:34:07 was logged with query_duration_ms=2, read_rows=10,000 and read_bytes=353,398 for a single result row, showing that at the current size even a keyed point lookup reads the whole table (one granule).

system.query_log held only 44 QueryFinish entries, spanning 2026-11-23 18:33:18 to 18:33:44, with a maximum query_duration_ms of 5 — the log retention visible in this Run is far too short to contain any earlier slow execution of the reported query.

Against the premise that this query is currently slow: the exact statement completed in 1 ms while reading 40,000 bytes, the whole orders table is only 142,755 bytes in one part, and a matching-value variant completed in 2 ms; the maximum duration recorded anywhere in the retained query_log was 5 ms.

The observed 10,000-row read is not specific to the customer_id predicate: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = 5000 on the sorting-key column also read 10,000 rows and 353,398 bytes, so at this data volume no measured latency or read-volume difference between a keyed lookup and the customer_id scan is observable.

Primary candidate: the ordering key of default.orders is 'id' only, so every customer_id filter must scan all granules (EXPLAIN: 'Condition: true', Granules 1/1); this makes per-lookup cost proportional to table size and is the mechanism by which this query becomes slow as orders grows, even though it is not slow at the current 10,000 rows.

Second candidate: the literal 12345 is outside the observed customer_id domain 1–1000, so this exact statement can never return a row and its whole scan is wasted work; the caller may be supplying the wrong identifier (for example an order id from a 0–9999 id range or another entity's key) — a parameter/correctness problem rather than a database-capacity problem.

Third candidate: SELECT * forces all five columns to be materialised once rows pass the filter — the matching-value run read 353,398 bytes versus 40,000 bytes for the no-match run — so projection width is a secondary contributor to per-query cost and it grows with added columns.

Fourth candidate: the user's slow experiences may involve a cost this Run cannot see (client/network wait, concurrent load, a different cluster or table, or a much larger historical data set), because query_log retention here covered only about 26 seconds of traffic.

Rejected as the explanation for slowness: part fragmentation or merge backlog on orders — the table has exactly one active part of 142,755 bytes, and the measured scans used about 3.1 MB of memory and 1–2 ms, showing no sign of over-fragmentation or memory pressure.

Fix the access path in ClickHouse terms by putting customer_id into the table's ordering key — for example rebuild as a new MergeTree with ORDER BY (customer_id, id) and INSERT SELECT from orders, or add a projection sorted by (customer_id, id) — then confirm with EXPLAIN indexes = 1 that the condition becomes 'customer_id in [...]' instead of 'Condition: true'.

If the existing ORDER BY id must be kept, add a data-skipping index suited to equality on a 1,000-value column (e.g. INDEX idx_customer_id customer_id TYPE set(1000) GRANULARITY n, or bloom_filter) as a stop-gap; note a skip index only avoids granules and is weaker than ordering by customer_id first, and my check of system.data_skipping_indices returned no rows so I could not confirm what skip indices exist today.

Replace SELECT * with an explicit column list (for example order_date, total_amount, status) to avoid reading all five columns; the measured matching-value run read 353,398 bytes versus 40,000 bytes for the filter-only run, so projection width is measurable.

Validate the customer_id parameter before sending it: the observed domain is 1–1000 while the failing statement used 12345, which cannot match any row; if the application expects orders for a customer, trace where 12345 comes from (order id vs customer id).

Before changing anything, capture real evidence of the slow runs: lengthen system.query_log retention and record query_duration_ms, read_rows, read_bytes, memory_usage and ProfileEvents for the failing executions so the before/after effect of any ordering-key change can be measured rather than assumed.

Client-side timing, connection pool behaviour and concurrency of the application issuing this query are not observable from the SQL source; whether the perceived slowness happens before or after the database statement completes is unknown.
